questions.question:
Consider the tree arcs of a BFS traversal from a source node W in an unweighted, connected,
undirected graph. The tree T formed by the tree arcs is a data structure for computing

options.A: the shortest path between every pair of vertices
options.B: the shortest path from W to every vertex in the graph.
options.C: the shortest paths from W to only those nodes that are leaves of T.
options.D: the longest path in the graph.

questions.explanation:
In an unweighted graph BFS visits vertices level by level from W, so the tree path from W to any vertex v has the minimum number of edges.

It does not give shortest paths between other pairs of vertices.

Answer: the shortest path from W to every vertex in the graph

questions.question: For parameters a and b, both of which are [latex]\omega(1) , T(n)=T(n^{1/a})+1[/latex], and [latex]T(b)=1[/latex]. Then [latex]T(n)[/latex] is
questions.explanation:
Each step takes the a-th root: [latex]n\rightarrow n^{1/a}\rightarrow n^{1/a^2}\rightarrow\cdots[/latex], until it reaches b.

[latex]n^{1/a^k}=b\Rightarrow\frac{\log_b n}{a^k}=1\Rightarrow k=\log_a\log_b n[/latex]

Each step adds 1, so [latex]T(n)=\Theta(\log_a\log_b n)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]\Theta(\log_a\log_b n)[/latex]

questions.question:
Given an integer array of size [latex]N[/latex], we want to check if the array is sorted (in either
ascending or descending order). An algorithm solves this problem by making a
single pass through the array and comparing each element of the array only with its
adjacent elements. The worst-case time complexity of this algorithm is
questions.explanation:
The algorithm compares each pair of adjacent elements once: [latex]N-1[/latex] comparisons in the worst case (when the array is actually sorted, it must check every pair before saying YES).

It cannot do less: any element not examined could break the order. So the worst case is [latex]\Theta(N)[/latex], i.e. both [latex]O(N)[/latex] and [latex]\Omega(N)[/latex].

Answer: both [latex]O(N)[/latex] and [latex]\Omega(N)[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.question:
An articulation point in a connected graph is a vertex such that removing the vertex and its incident edges disconnects the graph into two or more connected components.
Let T be a DFS tree obtained by doing DFS in a connected undirected graph G.
Which of the following options is/are correct?

options.A: Root of T can never be an articulation point in G.
options.B: Root of T is an articulation point in G if and only if it has 2 or more children.
options.C: A leaf of T can be an articulation point in G.
options.D: If u is an articulation point in G such that x is an ancestor of u in T and y is a descendent of u in T, then all paths from x to y in G must pass through u.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- The root is an articulation point exactly when it has two or more DFS children: there are no cross edges in an undirected DFS, so its subtrees connect only through the root [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (option 1 is FALSE).
- A leaf of T: removing it leaves the rest of T connected [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] never an articulation point [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Option 4: y's subtree may have a back edge to an ancestor above u (u is an articulation point because of another subtree), giving a path from x to y that avoids u [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Root of T is an articulation point iff it has 2 or more children

questions.question:
Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be an undirected, edge-weighted graph with integer weights. The weight of a path is the sum of the weights of the edges in that path. The length of a path is the number of edges in that path.

Let [latex]s \in V[/latex] be a vertex in [latex]G[/latex]. For every [latex]u \in V[/latex] and for every [latex]k \geq 0[/latex], let [latex]d_{k}(u)[/latex] denote the weight of a shortest path (in terms of weight) from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]u[/latex] of length at most [latex]k[/latex]. If there is no path from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]u[/latex] of length at most [latex]k[/latex], then [latex]d_{k}(u)=\infty[/latex].

Consider the statements:

S1: For every [latex]k \geq 0[/latex] and [latex]u \in V, d_{k+1}(u) \leq d_{k}(u)[/latex].

S2: For every [latex](u, v) \in E[/latex], if [latex](u, v)[/latex] is part of a shortest path (in terms of weight) from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]v[/latex], then for every [latex]k \geq 0, d_{k}(u) \leq d_{k}(v)[/latex].

Which one of the following options is correct?
questions.explanation:
[latex]d_k(u)[/latex] is the shortest-path weight from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]u[/latex] using at most [latex]k[/latex] edges — this is exactly the quantity computed by the Bellman-Ford relaxation process after [latex]k[/latex] rounds.

S1: [latex]d_{k+1}(u)\le d_k(u)[/latex] — allowing one extra edge of "budget" can only give access to more paths (a path of length [latex]\le k[/latex] is also a path of length [latex]\le k+1[/latex]), so the shortest weight can only stay the same or decrease. True, always.

S2: Suppose [latex](u,v)[/latex] lies on a shortest path from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]v[/latex]; then [latex]d(v)=d(u)+w(u,v)\ge d(u)[/latex] in the limit, so eventually [latex]d_k(u)\le d_k(v)[/latex] once [latex]k[/latex] is large enough. But for small [latex]k[/latex] this need not hold: it's possible that [latex]u[/latex] has not yet been reached with a short enough path (so [latex]d_k(u)=\infty[/latex] is even bigger) or, more subtly, that a different, cheaper path of length [latex]\le k[/latex] to [latex]v[/latex] exists that doesn't go through [latex]u[/latex] at all — the inequality can fail for some particular [latex]k[/latex] even though it eventually holds in the limit. So S2 is not always true for every [latex]k[/latex].

Answer: Only S1 is true.

questions.question: Consider a simple undirected weighted graph G, all of whose edge weights are distinct. Which of the following statements about the minimum spanning trees of G is/are TRUE?

options.A: The edge with the second smallest weight is always part of any minimum spanning tree of G .
options.B: One or both of the edges with the third smallest and the fourth smallest weights are part of any minimum spanning tree of G .
options.C: Suppose [latex]S\subseteq V[/latex] be such that [latex]S\neq  \phi [/latex] and [latex]S\neq  V[/latex] . Consider the edge with the minimum weight such that one of its vertices is in S and the other in V \ S . Such an edge will always be part of any minimum spanning tree of G .
options.D: G can have multiple minimum spanning trees.

questions.explanation:
With distinct weights the MST is unique (so option 4 is false).

- The two smallest edges cannot form a cycle, so Kruskal always takes both [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- If the 3rd smallest is rejected, it closes a triangle with the two smallest edges. Then the 4th edge cannot form a cycle with them (the triangle's 3 vertices are already fully joined), so it is taken [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- This is the cut property: the lightest edge crossing any cut is in every MST [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

questions.question:
Let [latex]G [/latex] be an edge-weighted undirected graph with positive edge weights. Suppose a positive constant [latex]\alpha [/latex] is added to the weight of every edge.
Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE about the minimum spanning trees (MSTs) and shortest paths (SPs) in [latex]G [/latex] before and after the edge weight update?

options.A: Every MST remains an MST, and every SP remains an SP.
options.B: MSTs need not remain MSTs, and every SP remains an SP.
options.C: Every MST remains an MST, and SPs need not remain SPs.
options.D: MSTs need not remain MSTs, and SPs need not remain SPs.

questions.explanation:
Adding the same positive constant [latex]\alpha[/latex] to every edge shifts the total weight of any spanning tree by exactly [latex]\alpha\times(n-1)[/latex] (since every spanning tree has exactly [latex]n-1[/latex] edges, the same count) — a uniform shift that doesn't change which spanning tree has the minimum total weight. So every MST remains an MST.

Shortest paths, however, can use a different number of edges depending on the route — a path with fewer edges gets a smaller total addition of [latex]\alpha[/latex] than a path with more edges, which can flip which path is actually shortest after the update. So SPs need not remain SPs.

Answer: Every MST remains an MST, and SPs need not remain SPs.

questions.question: Let G be a complete undirected graph on 4 vertices, having 6 edges  with weights being 1,2,3,4,5, and 6. The maximum possible weight that a minimum weight spanning tree of G can haveis .
questions.explanation:
An MST of 4 vertices has 3 edges; edges 1 and 2 are always taken (two edges cannot form a cycle).

To make the third edge as heavy as possible, put edges 1, 2, 3 in a triangle, so 3 is rejected. The 4th vertex must then be joined by the next lightest edge, 4.

Maximum MST weight = 1 + 2 + 4 = 7

Answer: 7
